design_note: Adds the arithmetic behind an operational signal. Four constructed error ratios share one availability objective, so readers can distinguish burn rate from raw failure percentage and from a safety exception.

source.title: Alerting on SLOs
source.publisher: Google SRE; Steven Thurgood and contributors
source.concept: Burn rate compares the observed bad-event ratio with the error allowance implied by the SLO. A value above one consumes that allowance faster than the target rate.
source.scope: Original ShopAssist rates and objective; no production measurements or recommended alert thresholds are claimed.

lesson.title: Turn failure percentage into budget burn
lesson.intro: ShopAssist has a constructed 99.5% request-availability objective. Compare four hypothetical, equally defined windows. Their bad-event allowance is 0.5%; unauthorized effects remain a separate hard incident condition.

data.rule: Burn = observed failure ratio / 0.005. This is availability, not an authority budget.

read: All bars use the same request definition, objective and window length.
A 1% failure ratio means twice the allowance rate, not one unit of burn.
The chart cannot convert a forbidden refund into an acceptable availability error.
lesson.question: At 2.5% failed requests, what is burn rate, and does it authorize five forbidden refunds?
lesson.answer: The burn rate is 2.5 / 0.5 = 5 times the target allowance rate. It does not authorize any forbidden refund. Availability budgets describe an operating objective; an observed unauthorized effect triggers its own containment rule. Alert decisions also need the declared windows, traffic and response policy.
lesson.takeaway: Normalize operational error ratios before comparing them; keep authority violations outside tolerable error budgets.
lesson.assumption: Constructed request rates over equal windows; no traffic-volume projection, alert threshold, safety allowance or measured service result is implied.
